## 1. GLOBAL MACRO OVERVIEW

The macro backdrop in late May 2026 is dominated by the geopolitical shock emanating from the US-Iran conflict that erupted in February 2026. The war's principal market transmission mechanism is energy: the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz — through which approximately one-fifth of global energy supplies normally transit — has driven oil prices sharply higher, stoked multi-year high inflation, and compressed real household incomes. The IMF, World Bank, and IEA issued a rare joint statement Friday warning that "global oil inventories are being drawn down at a record pace" and flagging the risk of summer fuel scarcity if shipping through Hormuz does not normalise [Source: https://www.globalvillagespace.com/imf-world-bank-iea-chiefs-warn-of-summer-fuel-scarcity-if-hormuz-strait-remains-closed/].

US inflation data released Thursday confirmed the escalating price pressure. The PCE price index rose 0.4% month-on-month in April after a 0.7% surge in March, with goods prices up 0.7% and gasoline and energy products surging 5.5%. Core PCE rose to 3.3% year-on-year in April from 3.2% in March — well above the Fed's 2% target and at the fastest pace in three years [Source: https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-28/us-inflation-firming-iran-war-drives-prices]. The broader CPI reading stands at 3.95% YoY as of April [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CPIAUCSL], while the 10-year Treasury yield sits at 4.45% and the 2-year at 3.99%, leaving the yield curve modestly positive [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS10].

Federal Reserve officials are increasingly hawkish. Governor Bowman, speaking at a conference in Iceland Friday, signalled she would "consider shifting my approach to thinking about the balance of risks" — a clear signal of potential rate hike bias — if the war-driven energy shock proves persistent [Source: https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-05-29/more-fed-policymakers-eye-possible-rate-hike-inflation-risks-rise]. The effective Fed Funds rate stands at 3.64% [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS], and markets are digesting the reality that cuts are firmly off the table and hikes are being discussed. The ECB faces a parallel dilemma: markets are pricing a ~91% probability of a 25bp hike at the June 11 meeting, which would take the deposit facility rate to 2.25%, with a 50% chance of another hike in September [Source: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/05/29/the-ecb-is-debating-rate-hikes-but-the-private-sector-could-help-out.html].

Despite these headwinds, equity markets have shown surprising resilience. US indices hit record highs intraday this week on alternating waves of Iran deal optimism before retreating as fresh military exchanges rekindled uncertainty. The VIX has pulled back to 15.32, down 2.67% [Source: Yahoo Finance (^VIX)], suggesting markets are pricing a contained conflict resolution rather than a structural escalation. The S&P 500 sits at 7,580.06, the Nasdaq 100 at 30,333.18, and the Dow at 51,032.46 — all registering modest gains [Source: Yahoo Finance (^GSPC, ^NDX, ^DJI)]. Asian markets were notably strong, led by KOSPI's 3.55% surge to 8,476.15 and Nikkei's 2.53% rally to 66,329.5 [Source: Yahoo Finance (^KS11, ^N225)]. Approximately 94% of chief economists surveyed now expect global inflation to rise further due to Hormuz disruption, while 87% expect global growth to weaken over the coming year [Source: https://www.hotelnewsresource.com/article141428.html].
